e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who lived or worked in a royal forest, woodland set aside for hunting. Forest is the single-r spelling.
namesakes: Forrest Gump (title character of the 1994 Tom Hanks film)

assoc.t: Forrest Gump, hero of the 1994 Tom Hanks film

e.note: Expect to hear 'Run, Forrest, run!' from Forrest Gump.

e.meaning: form of Helen, often explained as torch or shining light
e.etymology: An Old French form of Helen, from Greek Helene. In Arthurian legend Elaine of Astolat dies for love of Lancelot, and Tennyson's Idylls of the King (1859) revived the name.
namesakes: Elaine Benes (Julia Louis-Dreyfus's character on Seinfeld)
Elaine May (comedian and film director)
Elaine Chao (former US labor and transportation secretary)

assoc.t: Elaine Benes of Seinfeld

e.etymology: A pet form of Harriet, the English form of French Henriette, which comes from Henry, Germanic 'home ruler'. It has long been given as a full name.
namesakes: Hattie McDaniel (first Black Oscar winner, for Gone with the Wind)

e.etymology: A double-l spelling of Liliana, the Italian and Spanish form of Lilian, a name linked to Latin lilium, 'lily'.
A modern American spelling of Adeline, the French pet form of Adele, from the Germanic word adal, 'noble'.
From an English place name, Old English Wines tun, 'the farm of a man named Wine', a name meaning 'friend'. It was a Churchill family name long before the prime minister made it famous.
namesakes: Winston Churchill (British prime minister during World War II)
Winston Smith (hero of George Orwell's 1984)
Winston Zeddemore (the fourth Ghostbuster)

assoc.t: Winston Churchill, Britain's wartime prime minister
Winston cigarettes
Winston, the gorilla scientist in Overwatch

e.etymology: A name with several unrelated sources, among them a Bulgarian pet form of Rayna and a Russian pet form of Raisa. Disney's Raya and the Last Dragon (2021) lifted it in the US.

assoc.t: heroine of Disney's Raya and the Last Dragon

e.meaning: from the Roman family name Sergius, of unknown meaning
e.etymology: The Spanish and Italian form of Sergius, an old Roman family name that may be Etruscan. Saint Sergius, a 4th-century soldier martyr, spread it among Christians.
namesakes: Sergio Leone (director of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly)
Sergio Garcia (Masters-winning golfer)

e.etymology: From Greek melissa, 'honeybee', from meli, 'honey'. In Greek myth Melissa was a nymph who nursed the infant Zeus on honey.
namesakes: Melissa McCarthy (comedic actress)
Melissa Joan Hart (star of Sabrina the Teenage Witch)
Melissa Etheridge (rock singer)

assoc.t: hurricane that devastated Jamaica in 2025

e.etymology: Originally a medieval variant of Jack, now mostly a short form of Jacob, from Hebrew Yaakov, traditionally 'supplanter'.
namesakes: Jake Gyllenhaal (actor)
Jake Paul (YouTuber turned boxer)
Jake Tapper (CNN anchor)

assoc.t: Jake from State Farm, the insurance ad pitchman
Jake the Dog of Adventure Time

e.meaning: garden or orchard (from Carmel); also Latin for song
e.etymology: From the Spanish title of Mary, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, after the mountain whose Hebrew name means 'garden' or 'orchard'; its form was shaped by Latin carmen, 'song'. Bizet's opera Carmen (1875) spread it abroad.
namesakes: Carmen Miranda (1940s singer famous for her fruit hats)
Carmen Electra (model and actress)
Carmen Sandiego (elusive thief of the geography games)

assoc.t: Carmen, Bizet's 1875 opera
Carmen Sandiego, globe-trotting thief of games and TV

e.etymology: The Greek form of Egyptian Men-nefer, 'enduring and beautiful', the ancient capital of Egypt. The Tennessee city was named for it in 1819, and the given name follows the city.

assoc.t: Tennessee city, home of the blues and Graceland
capital of ancient Egypt

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Juliet, a pet form of Julia, the feminine of the Roman family name Julius. It is the Spanish name of Shakespeare's Juliet.

e.meaning: feminine form of Alan, a Celtic name of uncertain meaning
e.etymology: A feminine form of Alan, a Celtic name that Bretons brought to Britain, and a variant spelling of Alana. It also echoes the Irish endearment a leanbh, 'child'.
The Spanish form of Paul, from the Roman family name Paulus, 'small' or 'humble'.
namesakes: Pablo Picasso (Spanish painter and co-founder of Cubism)
Pablo Neruda (Nobel Prize-winning Chilean poet)
Pablo Escobar (Colombian drug lord)

assoc.t: Pablo Picasso, the painter
Pablo Escobar, Colombian drug lord

e.meaning: of Demeter, the Greek goddess of the harvest
e.etymology: A short form of Demetria, the feminine of Demetrius, 'devoted to Demeter', the Greek goddess of the harvest. Actress Demi Moore brought it into English use.
namesakes: Demi Moore (actress, Ghost and The Substance)
Demi Lovato (pop singer)

assoc.t: actress Demi Moore and singer Demi Lovato

e.etymology: The French form of Sylvia, from Latin silva, 'forest'.

assoc.t: Sylvie, the Loki variant in Marvel's Loki series

e.etymology: The Latinized form of Hugh, from the Frankish word hugi, 'mind, thought, spirit'. It began as a short form of longer names such as Hubert.
namesakes: Hugo Weaving (actor, The Matrix and The Lord of the Rings)
Hugo Chávez (former president of Venezuela)
Hugo Cabret (boy hero of the film Hugo)

assoc.t: Victor Hugo, author of Les Misérables
hurricane that struck South Carolina in 1989
Hugo, the Hugo Boss fashion line
Hugo Awards for science fiction and fantasy

e.etymology: A spelling of Cameron used mostly for girls. Cameron is the Scottish clan surname from Gaelic cam, 'crooked', and sròn, 'nose'. Actress Camryn Manheim brought the spelling to notice in the 1990s.
namesakes: Camryn Manheim (Emmy-winning actress, The Practice)

e.etymology: A spelling of Aniya, a modern American name that took off around 2000 beside Aaliyah and Anaya. Its source is not settled.
From Arabic Aishah, 'living, alive', from the verb asha, 'to live'. Aisha, daughter of the first caliph Abu Bakr, was a wife of the Prophet Muhammad.
namesakes: Aisha (wife of the Prophet Muhammad)
Aisha Tyler (actress and talk show host)

assoc.t: Aisha, wife of the prophet Muhammad

e.etymology: A Turkish name meaning 'moon halo', built on ay, 'moon'. In the US it is also popular with Spanish-speaking families.
From Arabic malik, 'king', and the related malik, 'owner, master'. Al-Malik, 'the King', is one of the names of God in Islam. In the US the name has long been popular with Black families.
From a Scottish surname and place name, from Gaelic caol, 'narrow', used for a strait or channel. Kyle is a district of Ayrshire.
namesakes: Kyle Chandler (actor, Friday Night Lights)
Kyle Busch (NASCAR champion)
Kyle Broflovski (one of the four boys of South Park)

assoc.t: meme name for a rowdy, energy-drink-fueled young man
Kyle, one of the four boys of South Park

e.note: Internet memes cast Kyle as a rowdy teen who chugs Monster energy drinks and punches drywall.

e.meaning: short form of Alana or of Russian Svetlana, light
e.etymology: A short form of Alana, or from Russian Lana, a pet form of Svetlana and similar names. Actress Lana Turner made it familiar in the 1940s.
namesakes: Lana Del Rey (singer-songwriter)
Lana Turner (1940s Hollywood star)
Lana Condor (actress, To All the Boys I've Loved Before)
e.note: Spelled backward it reads as a crude word, which sometimes draws jokes.

assoc.t: Lana Del Rey, singer-songwriter

e.etymology: From Medieval Latin Franciscus, 'Frenchman', the nickname of Saint Francis of Assisi, whose merchant father traded in France. His fame carried the name across Europe.
namesakes: Pope Francis (head of the Catholic Church, 2013 to 2025)
Francis Ford Coppola (director of The Godfather)
Francis Scott Key (wrote The Star-Spangled Banner)

assoc.t: Pope Francis, pope from 2013 to 2025

e.etymology: From Arabic amir, 'prince, commander', with the ending -i: 'princely'. It is a Persian and Arabic surname. Poet Amiri Baraka took it as his first name, and the Los Angeles fashion label Amiri raised its profile.
namesakes: Amiri Baraka (poet and playwright)

assoc.t: Amiri, the Los Angeles luxury fashion label

e.etymology: A spelling of Rowan, from the surname and the rowan tree with its red berries. Rowan is also the English form of Irish Ruadhán, 'little red-haired one'.
From Old Norse Ástríðr, from áss, 'god', and fríðr, 'beautiful, beloved'. A name of Scandinavian queens and princesses, borrowed into English in the 19th century.
namesakes: Astrid Lindgren (Swedish author of Pippi Longstocking)
Astrid Hofferson (Viking heroine of How to Train Your Dragon)

assoc.t: Astrid, the heroine of How to Train Your Dragon

e.etymology: From an English and Scottish surname for a scribe, secretary or cleric, from Old English clerc and Latin clericus. It has been a first name since the 1600s.
namesakes: Clark Gable (star of Gone with the Wind)
Clark Kent (Superman's alter ego)
Clark Griswold (dad of National Lampoon's Vacation)

assoc.t: Clark Kent, Superman's mild-mannered alter ego
Clarks, British shoe brand

e.etymology: An English spelling of the Welsh name Rhys, usually taken to mean 'ardor' or 'enthusiasm' and borne by medieval Welsh princes. It reached first-name use by way of the surname.

assoc.t: sounds like Reese's, the peanut butter cup candy

e.etymology: A feminine form of William, shortened from Wilhelmina and recoined in 19th-century America from Will. William joins Germanic wil, 'will, desire', and helm, 'helmet, protection'.
namesakes: Willa Cather (author of My Ántonia and O Pioneers!)
